The centre will develop technologies designed to help networks self-configure, self-heal, optimise performance, reduce energy consumption and improve operational efficiency.

The announcement comes as Saudi Arabia accelerates its digital transformation agenda under Vision 2030, the national strategy launched to diversify the economy beyond oil, foster innovation, develop local talent and position the Kingdom as a leading technology and investment destination.

AI takes centre stage in network operations

As communications service providers face growing pressure to support AI applications, cloud services, industrial digitisation and increasingly complex network environments, automation is becoming a critical requirement rather than a future aspiration.

Nokia’s Riyadh-based teams will specialise in developing service management and orchestration (SMO), self-organising networks (SON), autopilot capabilities and rApps, and software applications designed to automate network operations in open and intelligent network architectures.

These technologies aim to reduce the need for manual intervention in network management while improving service quality and energy efficiency. By applying AI to network operations, operators can automate routine processes, detect and resolve faults faster, optimise network performance in real time and reduce operational costs.

The centre will also explore AI-native technologies that could form part of future 6G networks, helping prepare communications infrastructure for the next generation of connectivity.

Mikko Lavanti, president of Middle East and Africa at Nokia, said AI is transforming industries and increasing the importance of advanced communications infrastructure: “AI is reshaping every industry, and networks are the critical infrastructure that will make that transformation possible.

“Our new R&D centre in Riyadh will bring Nokia’s global expertise together with Saudi talent to develop AI-powered automation that makes networks more autonomous, efficient and responsive. It also strengthens the Kingdom’s role in creating connectivity innovation for customers in Saudi Arabia and around the world.”

Supporting Saudi Arabia’s digital ambitions

The launch follows an agreement announced earlier this year between Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT) and Nokia president and CEO Justin Hotard, highlighting the growing collaboration between global technology providers and the Kingdom’s digital ecosystem.

The investment aligns closely with Saudi Vision 2030, which identifies digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence and knowledge-based industries as key pillars of future economic growth.

title: Agentic AI governance: A Computer Weekly Downtime Upload podcast
raw_text:
For Rashmi Shetty, vice president of enterprise AI at Capital One, governance is the next phase of large-scale artificial intelligence (AI) deployments, once organisations have established a technical blueprint and a data strategy.

She says the bank is committed to protecting the privacy of consumers, which means giving consumers confidence in Capital One’s ability to safeguard their personal and financial information. As the bank expands its data-enabled tech and AI capabilities, she says: “We believe it's important to have a privacy-focused mindset and build an environment where consumer data is safe, secure, and under the consumer's control.”

When deploying AI models, one of the decisions IT leaders need to make is how and when to use publicly available large language models (LLMs). It is generally safer to limit usage only to models that run internally. But these can limit the flexibility of having an LLM that has a greater understanding from knowledge accessed from the wider internet.

Even when models are run internally, inside the corporate network, whenever a public LLM is accessed, any queries submitted to it will be incorporated into the model’s understanding of the world, and is potentially available to anyone. If sensitive data is included in that query, this constitutes a data leak, which is why some organisations are focusing purely on internally run models and have chosen to ban the use of public LLMs.

However, rather than limiting the use of AI models only to the ones that can be run internally inside the company’s network, Shetty sees an opportunity to use governance to control how publicly available LLMs can be directed to work towards a specific business outcome. 

Capital One has worked on modernising its tech stacks and data ecosystem. Alongside these efforts, Shetty says it has also modernised and recalibrated risk and compliance and policy management based on a modern data ecosystem.

Among the main areas of concern for organisations looking at AI governance is personally identifiable information (PII) and ensuring there are General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) controls around that data.

As enterprise AI is deployed, there will be opportunities for standalone AI systems to collaborate in order to streamline business processes. The challenge in governance for agentic AI systems is ensuring each AI system required to run an end-to-end business process only has access to the data it needs to finish its bit of the task.

Shetty says this involves managing how data flows along an agentic trajectory, where data is passed between the different agentic AI systems that need to be accessed to achieve the specific task. She says that an agentic AI governance framework should define nuanced, atomic policies across this trajectory.

At Capital One, the  governance framework has been developed on top of the bank’s platform strategy and it is being updated to support agentic AI. “We are bringing it together for managing agency for our multi-agentic system,” Shetty adds.

This governance framework provides the guardrails for protecting personally identifiable information and GDPR controls.

In effect, the  governance framework defines what the agentic system that is powered by LLMs is allowed to do in terms of the tools and data it can access. The overall goal is a greater level of autonomy as Shetty explains: “You're taking a highly stochastic, probabilistic system, which can make dynamic decisions and trying to define a deterministic boundary using a safety and governance mechanism in order to increase your velocity towards autonomous decision-making.”

title: CW@60: In the flow - how AI brought back the magic of coding
raw_text:
On 22 September 2026, Computer Weekly turns 60. To mark the milestone, we asked some of our friends - experts, parliamentarians, IT leaders and suppliers - for their perspectives on how tech has changed their lives over six decades. What's changed the most for you since then?

I’ve had three distinct moments in my life where technology felt like pure magic.

The first was as a kid, watching a neighbour type a basic command into a Commodore VIC-20 to print “Hello” on the screen. The second was discovering the internet. The third was my first interaction with a large language model.

That first spark of magic led me to an Atari 800XL. As a 12-year-old, I set out to code a basic civilisation economics game, something even simpler than The Oregon Trail.

But there was a catch - for the first six months, I didn't have a floppy drive. Every single night, when I turned the machine off, I lost everything I had built. If I wanted to start a different project, I had to wipe the slate clean anyway, because there simply wasn't enough memory.

Looking back, those limitations taught me about patience, the reality of constraints, and the pure, childlike magic of creation. It taught me that following instructions to make a machine execute a vision is a profoundly rewarding experience.

The era of simple flow

Any lifelong builder, writer, or creative instantly understands the flow state. It is that deeply productive, highly rewarding zone where the outside world fades away and you are completely immersed in the act of creation.

During the early days of building the Sage Intacct platform, my environment was incredibly simple. I coded in Emacs, using simple terminal shells and basic print-line debugging. I didn’t have sophisticated tools telling me where things were broken - I would just force the code to halt and print out the state of a variable.

Because the environment was simple, getting into the flow was seamless. But you couldn’t find that flow in a 30-minute window between meetings, and it was shattered if someone stopped by my desk to ask me to approve an expense report.

To protect that state, our engineering team would often escape the corporate office. We’d go to someone’s house, sit around a fire at night, and code collectively for hours. Those uninterrupted, blissful sessions remain some of my fondest professional memories.

The barrier of accidental complexity

I then transitioned into the global chief technology officer (CTO) role at Sage – and was eventually forced to leave hands-on building behind. But it wasn't just the demands of my job that built a wall between me and the code - it was the evolution of the software industry itself.

For the last 40 years, our industry has relentlessly pursued developer productivity. Cloud computing, open source libraries, and advanced debuggers have driven massive acceleration. But that progress came with a heavy cost - accidental complexity.

“It is an incredibly exciting time to enter computer science, but it comes with a vital caveat for tomorrow’s software engineers”

Aaron Harris

Over time, developers began spending less of their day writing code and more of their time stitching complex systems together. You had to decide which libraries to use, configure intricate development environments, and manage a web of third-party APIs and dependency checkers.

The barrier to entry for the flow state became incredibly high. For a CTO with a seriously demanding day job, finding the hours just to set up an environment, understand the tooling, and link the dependencies was impossible. The upfront plumbing killed the joy of building, keeping me out of the builder’s seat for years.

Abracadabra – it’s AI

This is where agentic AI completely changed the game. Modern AI agents haven't just accelerated coding - they have bypassed the wall of complexity entirely. Today, an AI agent understands the tooling, manages the dependencies, and configures the environment on my behalf. Often, I don’t even need to look at the setup.

Instead, I can start having a conversation with a coding agent about what I want to build, and almost instantly, I slip back into that flow state. If I have an idea for a prototype, I don’t have to spend a weekend configuring a development environment. I can just start creating again. It has given me back that Atari 800XL feeling of magic.

There is also a bizarre, vintage paradox to this new era of AI development. To build the future, we are suddenly back to living in terminal command lines, writing shell scripts, and working in markdown files. It feels remarkably nostalgic, like software development 25 years ago, but supercharged.

A warning for the next generation

It is an incredibly exciting time to enter computer science, but it comes with a vital caveat for tomorrow’s software engineers.

While AI can handle the plumbing, the next generation of developers must still learn the fundamental mechanics of software engineering. You cannot effectively oversee software development – which is now happening at 10 times the speed – if you do not understand the core principles.

When you partner with a coding agent, it will make decisions about libraries, user interface frameworks, and logic. If you lack a fundamental understanding of how software works, you won't have the context to interrogate those decisions, ask the right questions, or recognise when the AI is drifting away from the required outcome.

AI is not here to replace the joy of creation. When governed by human expertise and built on a foundation of trust, it removes the friction and complexity that stand in our way. It allows us to focus on the outcomes, the logic, and the vision. Most importantly, it gives all of us a clear path back to the flow.

Aaron Harris is CTO at Sage.

title: Working with your board around risk – why cyber responsibility can’t be shirked
raw_text:
Earlier this year, the UK Government launched its Cyber Resilience Pledge initiative, aimed at encouraging more companies to invest in cyber security. This initiative aims to make those in charge of companies more aware of the challenges that affect their business operations, and how they have to make their systems more resilient.

The challenge around cyber security is making it relevant for board teams. IT is essential to how businesses operate today – according to Accenture’s Pulse of Change report, 71% of leaders rank investment in digital tools as their top strategy for managing operations. At the same time, the company found that 87% of organizations see cyber disruption as a recurring operating reality too.

Security problems are growing

The number of issues is growing too. According to our research, the number of critical vulnerabilities in the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list has gone up by 6.5 times since 2022, rising to 473 million issues closed in 2025. The other significant change for IT and business teams is around AI. Frontier AI models like Mythos and ChatGPT 5.5 Cyber perform well at finding issues in software. As part of its Project Glasswing initiative, Mythos discovered around 23,000 vulnerabilities, of which around 6,000 were rated as high or critical. AI can also be used to test and link those vulnerabilities together to become more serious attack chains.

In our research, we found more than 1,000 attack paths that took multiple issues and created potential exploits using AI. The attack paths would use issues rated as 7.0 or lower in severity, so they would be more likely to stay unpatched for longer. All of these issues - and there are a lot of them - threaten how security teams manage patching and configuration management. People can’t keep up.

The response to this has to be automation. Deploying updates automatically for low-risk issues can cut a lot of the overhead, leaving more time for humans to work on the issues that need insight or additional testing. The challenge for IT teams is trust around those updates. To solve this level of problem, teams can implement more automated processes for testing issues before deployment. Of more than 150 million patches deployed last year at our customers, 40 million were completed automatically, with only 0.01 percent rolled back.

Understanding risk, not just threats

For management teams and boards, these technical issues might seem like they are not important enough to merit individual attention. They would be right. But each one can also have a huge impact on how a business operates, bringing down IT systems or leading to financial losses.

For boards, understanding cyber risk in context is critical. The Cyber Resilience Pledge includes a commitment that board members should understand cyber security threats through undertaking NCSC Cyber Governance training. The board also has to go through a risk assessment exercise that asks for suppliers to get Cyber Essentials accreditation for themselves, with suppliers rated based on the company’s overall risk appetite.

This exercise should help board members get familiar with how to understand cyber security risk in theory. However, the sheer volume of potential issues that are coming up is overwhelming. Even with this training, board members need help to put these risks into perspective and context. For the IT team, the most effective way to do this is through estimating financial impact for any potential risk alongside the likelihood that this issue can be exploited.

Behind this, security teams can understand what the biggest risks are for the business based on real time insight and threat intelligence. If and when a serious issue does arise, that vulnerability can receive the attention that it needs. For the board, this risk figure should describe how much that vulnerability could cost as well as how effective any existing security controls are at preventing issues. Putting this in terms of cash at risk will make the board pay attention, as well as putting those losses into the same context as their other business decisions.

Once these issues are costed, the cash impact can be judged against each other. The board can then make decisions around potential losses and risk, and decide whether they will invest more to prevent that risk or to use other forms of capital like cyber insurance to hedge against that risk. On top of this, CISOs can take their boards through how they can design business processes to be more resilient.

Resilience involves more than simply protecting IT systems against attack, but where the overall system can carry on running even when something does go wrong. When companies rely on their digital strategies to work and face more threats, they have to invest in the right places to keep their operations functioning.  When AI can discover more issues and speed up how fast those issues are exploited, it is impossible to respond to every issue in advance. While CISOs often feel like they carry all the responsibility for cyber and IT security across their organisations, the reality is that directors and board members hold that duty. The solution to this problem is for CISOs to build up more resilience in their company systems, to automate the process around removing issues where possible, and to explain where risk exists in ways that the business can understand and make decisions on.

title: Activist takes data protection watchdog to court after Europol ‘unlawfully’ processed personal data
raw_text:
A human rights activist is bringing a legal case against Europe’s data protection watchdog for failing to protect her rights after her personal data was “unlawfully” stored and processed by the European policing agency, Europol.

Natalie Gruber, an Austrian campaigner who was targeted by Greek law enforcement after documenting Greece’s treatment of migrants, claims that Europol stored and collected her personal data with no valid legal basis.

She is bringing a case against the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) at the Court of Justice of the European Union, for failing to exercise the minimum due diligence to investigate her claim against Europol.

The activist said that she was forced to shut down an organisation she co-founded to support migrants and to abandon her humanitarian work after being subjected to a campaign of “lawfare” by Greek law enforcement.

According to the complaint, Gruber has also obtained prima facie evidence that the European border agency, Frontex, collected information about her during “debriefing interviews” with failed asylum seekers and shared it unlawfully with Europol.

She is asking the court to overturn a decision by EDPS that found that Europol had acted lawfully by storing and processing her personal data, and is seeking €130,000 in compensation.

Europol and Frontex ‘shielded from scrutiny’

Iftach Cohen, co-director of Front-Lex, a campaign group which is backing Gruber’s case against the EDPS, said that the inability of the data protection regulator to properly perform its role shielded Europol and the European border agency, Frontex, from scrutiny.          

“Europol was willing to break EU data protection law and support an evident campaign of lawfare … because of the nature of her humanitarian work. The EDPS has disgracefully shielded Europol and Frontex for the very same reason,” he added.

Gruber, an Austrian citizen, co-founded Josoor International Solidarity in 2016 to support migrants who had been subject to “pushback” operations, in which countries force migrants back across a border without giving them a chance to present their case or claim asylum.

In 2020, she learned that she and other human rights defenders were being investigated by Greece’s anti-terrorism police, secret service and coast guard over allegations of espionage and facilitating the illegal entry of foreigners into Greek territory.

According to Front-Lex, Greek law enforcement agencies made the accusations at a time when they faced growing criticism over their systematic pushbacks of migrants from Greece to Turkey, which were being monitored and recorded by Gruber and other activists.

Natalie Gruber, photographed in 2020 when conducting monitoring and reporting work on migrant pushbacks in the Evros region in Greece. Source: Natalie Gruber

Europol processed and stored Gruber’s personal data both during the Greek investigation and long after it had ended, and linked Gruber to the alleged crime of “aiming at forcing the competent border authorities to rescue the migrants”, according to the complaint.

The data collected by Europol included Gruber’s date of birth, her address in Austria, the fact that she lacked of criminal record in Austria and her role as president of Josoor. She was described as a “contact” linked to “illegal immigration and other organised crime”.

Europol disclosed that it had processed the data in relation to a preliminary inquiry into alleged offences including forming and joining a criminal organisation, espionage, violation of state secrets and facilitation of illegal immigration.

No legal basis

According to the complaint, Europol had no legal basis to process Gruber’s data when it manifestly related to non-criminal activity.

It argues that a member state cannot make processing of data lawful by labelling it “organised crime” when the underlying conduct was documenting human rights violations and calling on authorities to fulfil their legal duties.

Gruber complained to the European Data Protection Supervisor in 2022, challenging Europol’s processing of her personal data and its failure to disclose her data under subject access request.

By the time the charges against her were formally dropped in February 2024, the EDPS had still not “diligently investigated” her complaint or issued a decision and Europol continued to process her data. It took the EDPS a further 13 months to notify Europol that Gruber was no longer facing charges, after she alerted the regulator. 

    The EDPS issued a decision to reject Gruber’s complaint more than three and a half years after she filed it, without issuing the minimum due diligence required to protect her rights as a data subject, the complaint alleged.

    Gruber also alleged that there were concrete reasons to suspect that her personal data may have been processed in “parallel IT systems” at Europol – revealed in an investigation by Computer Weekly, Correctiv and Solomon – that failed to meet security and data protection standards.

    Cohen said that Gruber was targeted with a campaign of “lawfare” for assisting refugees and migrants, adding that Europol continued processing Gruber’s personal data for 18 months after the Greek investigation had found no evidence of any crime.

    “It stopped only after the EDPS passed on the information Natalie [Gruber] herself had provided about her acquittal – but the EDPS had sat on that information for a full year before forwarding it to Europol. During that year, [Gruber] was left believing that there must be another criminal investigation underway against her somewhere in Europe,” he added.

    Timeline

    May 2020 – Gruber became aware that Greek authorities had launched a criminal investigation into her and her organisation, Josoor International Solidarity.

    September 2020 – Greek police issue a press release on a joint investigation by the secret service, anti-terror police and the coast guard into four un-named NGOs. The investigation focused on allegations that Gruber and other human rights defenders were involved in a criminal organisation set up to conduct espionage and to facilitate illegal entry of foreigners into Greek territory and had engaged in those activities themselves.

    September 2021 – Gruber submitted data subject access requests (DSARs) to the Austrian Police, the Austrian Interior Ministry and Interpol, which quickly confirmed they held no information on her. She also submitted a DSAR to Europol.

    October 2021 – The UN special rapporteur on human rights defenders issued a statement in support of human rights defenders supporting migrants, refugees and asylum seekers in Greece. The rapporteur identified a “smear campaign” against defenders in the media and said the fear of arbitrary arrest had deterred some of the participants from carrying out human rights work and offering humanitarian aid at the border of the European Union.

    May 2022 – Europol refuses Gruber’s DSAR “in order to guarantee that any national investigation will not be jeopardised”.

    June 2022 – The UN special rapporteur on human rights defenders criticised the criminalisation of humanitarian assistance, including rescue operations for those in distress at sea, to people arriving on Greek islands. She warned that criminal investigations into human rights defenders was undermining their work and called for Greece to end the misuse of criminal law.

    October 2022 – Gruber, under pressure from threats of criminal investigation by Greek authorities, dissolved Josoor.

    November 2022 – Gruber filed a complaint with the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) asking it to look into Europol’s decision to refuse her DSAR and the lawfulness of Europol processing her personal data.

    April 2023 – An article in euobserver reported that the European border agency, Frontex and border guards in Greece were interrogating detained migrants during “debriefing interviews” and collecting information, including on the work of NGOs, which was shared with Europol.

    December 2023 – Gruber submitted a DSAR to Frontex.

    January 2024 – Frontex said it is unable to find any data on Gruber, but suggested she sends a subject access request to Europol, “considering that Frontex transfers operational personal data to them”.

    February 2024 – A Greek court dropped charges against Gruber and other aid workers.

    May 2024 – Gruber emailed EDPS to inform it that the criminal investigation against her had been closed and that she had been acquitted of all charges.

    June 2025 – EDPS informed Europol that Greece had dropped charges against Gruber, a year after Gruber had first alerted EDPS.

    July 2025 – Europol deleted the information Gruber had requested under her DSAR from its operational systems.

    September 2025 – Gruber wrote to EDPS setting out why Europol’s response failed to provide her with sufficient information, including which authorities had shared information about her with Europol and when the information was shared, and the lack of any assessment whether processing her data was lawful.

    May 2026 – Gruber submitted a further update to EDPS drawing attention to a report by Computer Weekly, Correctiv and Solomon, about Europol’s use of internal systems, known as the Computer Forensic Network and the “pressure cooker” to store data without adequate security or data protection safeguards.

    July 2026 – EDPS found that Europol was not in breach by processing Gruber’s personal data.

    September 2026 – Natalie Gruber brought a case against the EDPS at the European Court of Justice of the European Union.

title: HP grows Saudi presence through AI, manufacturing and skills investment
raw_text:
Saudi Arabia has become one of HP’s most strategic markets globally, with the company expanding its footprint across artificial intelligence, local manufacturing and skills development as part of its long-term commitment to the Kingdom’s Vision 2030 agenda.

According to Fadle Saad, managing director of HP’s MENA regional headquarters, the company’s investments are closely aligned with Saudi Arabia’s ambitions to build a diversified, knowledge-based economy capable of attracting global talent, technology investment and advanced manufacturing capabilities.

“Capacity building and capability building really summarises what Vision 2030 is about,” said Saad. “Saudi Arabia has a vision that is pragmatic, detailed and understood across society. That is something that strongly resonated with HP and influenced how we developed our strategy in the Kingdom.”

Over the past year, HP has reached several significant milestones. The company’s Riyadh manufacturing facility has moved into commercial production, with devices now being shipped to customers and partners across Saudi Arabia. At the same time, HP has expanded its education and workforce development initiatives and strengthened its AI research efforts through a dedicated research and development centre in the Kingdom.

Building local AI capabilities

A central pillar of HP’s Saudi strategy is the development of locally relevant AI solutions through its AI R&D Centre of Excellence. Rather than creating technologies in isolation, the centre works directly with customers and academic institutions to identify business challenges that can be addressed through AI. The model mirrors a successful HP R&D operation in Spain and is designed to combine customer insights, academic expertise and local talent.

“There are a lot of products that get born from a lab,” said Saad. “However, the whole idea of the HP research and development centre is to identify problems at the customer side and then work on solutions that could be relevant locally, regionally and internationally.”

One example is HP AgentOne, an agentic AI solution developed to address the inefficiencies associated with IT service management. The platform can automatically capture IT support requests from multiple channels, including email, voice interactions and direct employee requests, before routing or resolving issues autonomously.

The project emerged from customer workshops conducted with large organisations in Saudi Arabia, highlighting HP’s focus on practical business outcomes rather than AI experimentation alone. “We ask the billion-dollar question of whether AI can solve a specific problem,” said Saad. “Then we work with local academia and local talent to develop those solutions.”

The company is also investing in AI skills through the launch of the HP AI Academy, which aims to equip students, professionals and future workers with the capabilities needed in an increasingly AI-driven economy.

Alongside AI innovation, HP has made significant progress in local manufacturing. The company confirmed that its Saudi production facility is now commercially operational, marking a major step in its localisation strategy. Devices manufactured in Riyadh are already being delivered to customers and partners across the Kingdom.

Saad credited support from government entities, including the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT) and the Ministry of Investment, for helping accelerate the project.

“We were able to have a factory that is actually commercially producing today,” he said. “We have units right now being shipped to our customers and partners from our Saudi factory.”

For HP, manufacturing is closely linked to its AI ambitions. The company sees increasing demand for AI-enabled devices as organisations adopt new applications and productivity tools. “Every knowledge worker needs a device,” said Saad. “The more AI applications and productivity discussions arise, the more organisations need devices that can support them.”

AI adoption accelerates

Saudi Arabia’s rapid uptake of AI is creating favourable conditions for HP’s broader technology strategy.

According to Saad, both government and enterprise demand for AI solutions continue to grow at pace. He pointed to recent industry data showing that AI adoption among workers in Saudi Arabia has doubled year-on-year, reflecting how quickly organisations are integrating AI into day-to-day operations.

However, HP believes technology’s value extends beyond productivity gains. The company has increasingly focused on the relationship between technology and employee experience, arguing that better digital tools can improve workplace engagement and organisational culture.

“Technology is actually a contributor to the culture inside the organisation,” said Saad. “The better the technology and tools employees use, the happier they are in their environment.”

This philosophy is influencing both HP’s device strategy and its software development efforts, with AI increasingly being used to understand employee satisfaction and improve workplace experiences.

Supporting the next generation of innovators

Looking beyond enterprise customers, HP is also targeting Saudi Arabia’s growing startup ecosystem, with the launch of Garage 2.0, an incubator programme inspired by the original HP Garage in Palo Alto. The initiative is designed to bring together startups, educators, industry stakeholders and HP experts to support innovation and entrepreneurship in the Kingdom.

Saad believes the expansion of Saudi Arabia’s private sector and startup ecosystem will be one of the most significant outcomes of Vision 2030 and an area where HP can play a meaningful role.

“We see a much larger private sector contribution to the economy,” he said. “That naturally creates opportunities for startups to emerge and grow.”

Through Garage 2.0, HP aims to help aspiring entrepreneurs transform ideas into viable businesses while strengthening the innovation ecosystem around them. “It is a very intentional initiative from HP,” said Saad. “We want to help people move from being wannabe entrepreneurs to becoming actual startups.”

Growing alongside Vision 2030

As Saudi Arabia continues its economic transformation, HP expects its role in the Kingdom to expand further. The company sees ongoing infrastructure investments, growing AI adoption and a supportive regulatory environment creating new opportunities across technology development, manufacturing and innovation.

“We are growing with Vision 2030,” said Saad. “We are benefiting from the ecosystem that the government is establishing and facilitating, and we see significant opportunities to continue investing in Saudi Arabia’s future.”

For HP, the Kingdom is no longer simply a sales market. It is increasingly becoming a location where technologies are developed, products are manufactured, and future talent is nurtured, positioning Saudi Arabia as a key pillar of the company’s regional and global strategy.

title: Interview: The tech stack helping ‘q-commerce’ scale at Tesco
raw_text:
For many retailers, quick commerce (q-commerce) has been characterised by standalone technology stacks, dedicated fulfilment networks, and outsourced partnerships with third parties. The UK’s largest retailer, Tesco, has taken a markedly different route.

Rather than building a separate rapid delivery operation, the UK’s largest retailer has embedded its rapid delivery service, Whoosh, within its existing digital, fulfilment and store technology platforms. The result – five years from inception – is a proposition that is now accessible to more than 74% of the UK population and processes around 300,000 orders each week, while sharing core capabilities with Tesco’s wider online grocery operation.

Sales via Whoosh were up by 51% in the year to the end of February 2026, surpassing £400m.

Whoosh seemingly offers a case study in how enterprise retailers can scale new digital propositions without creating technical debt, duplicate platforms or organisational silos – three challenges often holding retailers back, as our recent interview with Ann Summers’ technology and supply chain director Jeannette Copeland underlined.

According to Kawaldeep Anand, head of product – digital customer experience (CX) for Whoosh and Tesco’s grocery home shopping division, the service’s success has been driven by building on Tesco’s existing technology estate rather than replacing it.

“Whoosh hasn’t been built as a separate proposition,” he says. “It has been built as part of our wider digital and store ecosystem.”

That philosophy has shaped every stage of the platform’s evolution over the past five years.

Platform thinking

As demand for rapid grocery delivery has accelerated, particularly during the coronavirus pandemic when partnerships such as Boots and Deliveroo and Asda and Uber Eats were established to cater to the unprecedented consumer need for q-commerce, Tesco resisted creating a standalone application, fulfilment platform or engineering organisation.

Instead, the retailer integrated Whoosh into the same customer-facing digital channels, core retail services and operational platforms already supporting its wider grocery business.

“This has allowed us to grow the service in a measured way using our existing store network, our familiar app and website, our Clubcard capabilities, our fulfilment technology and our delivery partner network,” Anand explains.

From a technology perspective, this has apparently created several advantages. Existing services could be reused, engineering investment benefited multiple business units simultaneously, and innovations developed for Whoosh could flow back into Tesco’s broader retail platform.

“It has given us a chance to test and refine the technology, improve the operating model, and to listen to colleagues and customer feedback along the way,” says Anand. “As a result, we’ve built a robust, resilient, scalable technology solution that benefits the whole Tesco Group rather than just a rapid delivery platform.”

A tech stack built largely in-house

At the centre of Whoosh sits a technology platform that Tesco has overwhelmingly developed internally.

“Almost the entire technology stack behind Whoosh, from customer-facing applications through to the APIs [application programming interfaces] that power the service, is bespoke and designed, built and managed by the Tesco Technology division,” says Anand.

The architecture comprises four primary layers. The CX layer delivers Whoosh through the existing Tesco mobile app and Tesco.com, allowing customers to use familiar payment methods, Clubcard functionality and digital journeys rather than switching to a separate rapid-commerce application.

Supporting this is the colleague and fulfilment layer, which connects store-based picking applications with Tesco’s retail and fulfilment platform. These services orchestrate inventory availability, pricing, payments, customer orders, routing, capacity planning, picking workflows and marshalling.

The third layer integrates external delivery providers, including Uber Eats, Just Eat and Stuart, through APIs that manage dispatch, collection, delivery tracking and customer notifications. As order volumes have increased, Tesco has continually evolved these integrations to improve resilience and operational scalability, according to Anand.

Completing the architecture is a data and analytics layer that provides operational visibility across customer demand, fulfilment efficiency and platform performance, allowing product and engineering teams to optimise capacity, improve CX, and identify opportunities for continuous improvement.

Third-party technology is used selectively where it provides clear value. For example, Tesco continues to use Worldpay as its payments gateway. However, Anand stresses that the core CX, fulfilment logic, orchestration services and Clubcard integration remain proprietary capabilities developed by Tesco Technology.

For Tesco, that level of ownership delivers an important strategic advantage – the ability to evolve rapidly without depending on supplier roadmaps or undertaking major platform replacements.

Stores for scale

Building the platform was only one challenge. Scaling it across hundreds of stores presented another.

Unlike rapid-commerce specialists built around dark stores, Tesco needed to enable physical stores to support traditional retail operations while simultaneously functioning as local fulfilment hubs.

“The store network is central to the model,” says Anand. “Stores are close to customers, they already hold the grocery inventory, and they are already part of their local communities.”

The engineering challenge therefore became one of orchestration rather than infrastructure.

“The technology challenge is to make that network even more responsive to their communities, so a store can serve customers shopping in person and ordering digitally.”

When Whoosh expanded into Tesco Express stores, the operational model became significantly more complex. Smaller footprints, reduced staffing levels and different workflows meant existing systems required adaptation rather than simple replication. Tesco responded by redesigning order-picking applications, colleague messaging and fulfilment workflows specifically for convenience stores.

The retailer also developed new catchment optimisation algorithms that balance customer demand, picking capacity and delivery partner availability to maximise fulfilment performance while protecting delivery promises.

Notably, these enhancements were introduced without deploying additional physical tech devices into stores, reducing implementation complexity and minimising operational disruption, according to Anand.

“If you needed evidence that rapid delivery can be successfully integrated into a wider retail operating model rather than treated as something separate from stores, we’re it,” he says.

Cross-functional product engineering

Whoosh’s organisational model mirrors its platform architecture.

What began as a small innovation team has evolved into multiple multidisciplinary squads spanning product management, engineering, programme delivery, user experience, experimentation, analytics and data science.

“The early 0-to-1 journey was driven by close collaboration between our business and Tesco Technology teams,” Anand explains.

Today, those teams own products throughout their lifecycle, enabling rapid experimentation alongside operational accountability.

“Our way of working is important. Whoosh is a live service operating at pace and scale, so these multidisciplinary teams own products and services end-to-end. They need to be able to experiment, iterate quickly, and work closely with store operations and business teams to solve practical challenges.”

Crucially, according to Anand, Tesco avoided creating isolated engineering capabilities for rapid commerce.

“We deliberately avoided creating a standalone technology stack for rapid delivery to make sure innovation flowed through the business both ways – from the wider business to Whoosh and vice versa,” he says.

AI accelerating product delivery

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly supporting both software delivery and operational optimisation across Tesco Technology.

“Our approach is practical, and we see it as a powerful tool as opposed to a standalone capability,” says Anand.

Within Whoosh, AI is already being applied throughout the product development lifecycle, supporting rapid prototyping, design analysis, insight generation, experimentation and testing.

“This helps our teams move from idea to evidence more quickly,” he adds.

Operationally, Tesco has already demonstrated measurable benefits. AI-enabled scheduling tools created an additional 100,000 online delivery slots in the week before Christmas, while Whoosh attracted more than 250,000 new customers in the same period, according to Anand.

Looking ahead, Tesco sees opportunities in AI-enabled product discovery, conversational commerce and shopping journeys delivered through messaging platforms including WhatsApp.

“The important point is that customers and colleagues may not always see AI directly,” says Anand. “Instead, they experience the benefits through services that feel more relevant, more reliable and easier to use.”

Business performance metrics

Tesco acknowledges the pace of rapid commerce demands a product operating model built around continuous delivery rather than periodic releases.

According to Anand, product managers spend their time balancing customer needs, engineering priorities and operational realities through constant collaboration with business, engineering, user research, data science and operations teams.

Ideas are validated through experimentation and A/B testing before broader deployment, ensuring product decisions remain evidence-based.

“The work is both practical and strategic, and success is measured by business performance metrics, not outputs,” he says.

As Whoosh enters its next phase of growth, Tesco’s priorities remain closely aligned with its platform strategy.

Expansion will focus on extending geographical coverage, increasing store participation, broadening the available product range and continuing to personalise the CX through data-driven capabilities. There is also a recognition within Tesco that rapid delivery itself is evolving.

“Rapid delivery started with emergency top-ups,” says Anand. “That’s still important, but customers are increasingly using Whoosh for broader baskets.”

The retailer is already experimenting with larger basket sizes and later same-day fulfilment in selected locations, creating new use cases that bridge traditional grocery delivery and immediate convenience shopping.

From a technology perspective, that evolution looks set to rely on the same architectural principles that have underpinned Whoosh since its 2021 launch.

“We will continue to make the experience more personalised and intuitive by making it easier to build baskets, improving access to Clubcard rewards and using data and customer insight responsibly to create a more relevant shopping experience,” Anand notes.

Tesco’s strategy demonstrates that rapid commerce, q-commerce, or speedy delivery – whatever a retailer refers to it as – does not necessarily require separate technology estates or independent operating models. Instead, by treating it as another capability within a common platform, Tesco has created an architecture supporting both innovation and long-term scalability – a crucial combination in a retail world that never stands still.

title: CW@60: The long gestation of a data nerd and agent overseer
raw_text:
On 22 September 2026, Computer Weekly turns 60. To mark the milestone, we asked some of our friends - experts, parliamentarians, IT leaders and suppliers - for their perspectives on how tech has changed their lives over six decades. What's changed the most for you since then?

I was born two years before Computer Weekly and for the first couple of decades of my life, our worlds did not intersect at all. I didn’t see a computer until I was 19 and working in a tool distribution company in Birmingham where we checked stock in and out on a green-screen mainframe.

I was a user, except occasionally I was roped into the daily routine of taking out the disks. The machines were the size of a washing machine, the disks a foot across, with a big clamp-and-close handle you swung shut. 

That was the extent of my IT life for another decade, during which I was a toolmaker in Birmingham, and my world was strictly Industry 1.0. There were CNC (computer numerical control) machines in the shop, but I had nothing to do with them beyond asking someone to make me a part now and then.

An access course carried me into university in my mid-twenties, and then I got my first computer: an Olivetti green screen with 5.25” disks. I used it to write essays. There was nothing else you could do with it.

After university - BA Middle East history, MSc Africa / Asia politics - I worked in journalism almost from the start, on various publications. I laid out pages and wrote articles on PCs and Macs. I was still very much a user.

Three or four years later, I got my first PC. I went on the internet via a noisy modem, and got into downloading music through Napster and Limewire. It opened a world of exploration I could not afford before, when a record meant money I did not really have.

Still a user

In 1997 my journey brought me to Computer Weekly. I worked there as a sub-editor, production editor, then reporter. My background dictated I would report on IT in manufacturing, so I covered ERP and MRP, visited oil refineries, the Longbridge car plant in Birmingham, an iron ore mine in Sweden. I was still a user of technology but becoming a professional observer too.

That phase lasted for seven years, before I went freelance and moved to the north of England.

Now I was responsible for my own PC, and I quickly learned to fix what went wrong. Two HDD failures in the space of months forced me to delve deeper into the guts of the PC and its components, and I soon became comfortable Googling my way through problems. 

By the late-2000s I had become storage editor for what would become soon Computer Weekly’s parent company. It was a space I’d largely adopted because everyone else considered it too boring.

I got to dive deeper into the tech, and was even given the chance to do a week’s course in storage technology certified by the industry body.

But in my relationship to IT, I was largely a user or an observer, and that held until the late 2010s.

The practitioner

Somewhere along the way, an interest in football – I was coaching our boy’s football team by this time – coincided with the rise of “citizen analysts” of football data. I was amazed at what people could do – turning raw football statistics into charts and graphics. And it resonated with me, because I never quite trusted my impressions when watching football and craved the grounding that numbers and patterns and arrows on a pitch graphic gave me.

“ Instead of being in the tactical weeds of coding or writing, I oversee an LLM-powered worker that can assess and summarise vast volumes of source material, locally and on the internet”

Antony Adshead

To do any of it, I needed software, so I taught myself R, the open source data science software. It was a long process – several months of pain simply learning it, and more when building things. When something did not work, my only recourse was Stack Overflow, and hoping someone's problem somewhere in the world had intersected with mine.

Sometimes a whole afternoon or a day slipped by before I found the fix for a single line holding everything up. But it was a great introduction to programming, because everything had to happen by hand. I also learned some Python.

That ability to fix computers and work with data soon collided with a newer part of my life: I had become a trustee for Mums In Need, the domestic abuse charity my wife started in 2014. It is a small organisation – fewer than 10 employees – but still has real IT requirements, and I became board member with special responsibility for IT, which gives some flavour of the concerns of a real CIO. I was the person with the hands-on knowledge of software and the strategic IT overview my work at Computer Weekly gave me.

One milestone, still ongoing, was the case management system I built for the caseworkers who support our service users. It runs on Google AppSheet, a low-code platform, and replaced a clunky, bought-in casework system that was far too widely scoped and never really suited the work Mums In Need actually did. Inevitably, shadow IT in the form of Google Sheets had grown up around it. What we wanted was to bring all that data together – to gather it, to build reports and, crucially, to build good evidence for the funding applications on which charities are utterly dependent.

So I moved from user and observer to practitioner – first tactically, learning R and doing data analysis as a football hobby – then doing data science for the charity and building software around data, and with the leadership remit an IT board member might hold in any organisation. Mums In Need is small and my work very part time, but the overhead is real and covers the gamut from data protection and data backup to developing systems to handle the organisation's information.

The agent overseer

The latest phase of my evolution has been as an everyday user of large language models (LLMs) in my role as acting datacentre and cloud editor with Computer Weekly, in particular when I have my data journalism hat on. 

I hesitate to call it AI. It’s a glorified autocomplete, even if the frontier models are very, very powerful. Really what we’re doing is leveraging LLMs, and at best and in the most critical environments, learning how to work with their limitations. 

I’d been using “one-shot” browser-chat AI for some time, but had long thought there must be a better way. You can set up persistent chats to guide Gemini or ChatGPT with a “master prompt” but it soon forgets what you tell it. You can get them to help writing R scripts for example, but they never truly know what you’re doing because they live in one window while Rstudio is in another. 

I knew “agentic” was the next big thing and that I needed AI to work more as a copilot – that is, literally having vision and the means to execute actions in the folders / environment I’m working in - but had struggled to gain any traction.

Two encounters really gave me a kick up the backside. I met a developer friend in the pub one night, where he told me of the work he had been doing with agentic AI. He had a job scraping some specific data from every council in the country. The scraper worked autonomously; if it encountered a failure, it rebuilt itself to work around the issue. It all worked with "skills" he said, and markdown files. I hadn't got a clue what he was talking about and felt like I'd arrived in a time machine from 1956.

A couple of weeks later I was at a Google event. A Google employee was sat next to me, laptop open on his knees during a keynote. I tried desperately to look as if I wasn’t looking and caught glimpses of a fleet of agents at work in different panes – researching, checking, working. I thought - I need to know how to do that.

A few months later – and taking inspiration from the likes of Jake Van Clief and Matt Pocock – a lot of my work revolves around an LLM inside a code editor, and using markdown-based workflow and skills files, that help me research, conduct data analysis, write drafts, and where needed, verify quotes and check facts.

It seems obvious to me that such setups are a good fit for many types of relatively unstructured work because the LLM provides the intelligence to bring structure. IDE-integrated, agentic workflows are commonplace in software engineering. If the enterprise can use such code editors to generate and maintain vast codebases, it is a dead-cert candidate for spheres such as research and article or report drafting, where the concept of “diffing” is easily transferable and possible at high speed and reliably with a capable LLM. 

The challenge is to keep the LLM on track through the ability to guide the workflow and to compensate for the context window and memory limitations that even frontier models carry.

The end result is a setup that allows me to handle vast amounts of information - multiple datasets of multiple types, PDFs, CSVs, markdown, whatever it can read. Meanwhile, its agentic capabilities can spin up R and Python scripts for intermediate checks or as part of persistent data pipelines for perpetual use. Via MCP servers it can carry out research on the internet and add to the dataset. Its outputs can be checked against source material and finished articles can be compared to its drafts so it can build your requirements into the markdown-based documents that guide its workflow.

Not yet the culmination

So, what’s my role as I do this? I feel sometimes I’ve become more like the editor now. I’m taking strategic decisions all day long. Instead of being in the tactical weeds of coding or writing, I oversee an LLM-powered worker that can assess and summarise vast volumes of source material, locally and on the internet. Its brain can work with far more sources than I can, so I guide it to investigate angles and report back, tweak lines of research on my instruction, edit its written and graphical outputs. 

But I am glad I learned to code before all this arrived, because to use an LLM for this kind of work it is essential to have some idea of what it is doing – to see where it might have gone wrong, and to troubleshoot when things do not come out as you expected. That depends on knowing what happens at the code window level. It’s the equivalent of knowing your subject matter when it comes to editorial decisions.

And so that’s where I’m at now in my journey in IT. It’d be foolish to call it a culmination. Things move so fast and who knows where we’ll be in a year’s time. I’m sure there’s a lot more I could explore.
